title: Law and story
hookLine: the Talmud mixes law (halakha) and story (aggadah) on the same page

cards: Rabbi Yose is on the road, and it's time to pray. He steps into a ruin, one of the broken buildings of Jerusalem, for a quiet corner. When he comes out, someone is waiting at the doorway.
It's Elijah the prophet, who has stood there patiently until the prayer was done. Elijah has two questions. Why did you go in there?
And then: my son, what did you hear? This story isn't in a book of tales. It sits in the middle of a discussion about the hours of the night.

teach.b: Aggadah. The Talmud's stories, sayings, parables and reflections: everything that isn't law. The law has its own name, halakha.
And here's the surprise for a first-time reader: they aren't in separate books. They share the page.

teach.h: A LEGAL QUESTION ABOUT THE NIGHT.
teach.b: Early in Berakhot, the sages are working out when the evening Shema may be said, and that leads to a question about how the night is divided into watches. A legal question, about time.
Then a sage teaches that at each watch of the night, God roars like a lion over the destroyed Temple. And right there, Rabbi Yose tells his story. Elijah's first words to him are practical.
Why go into a ruin? You could have prayed on the road, and if passersby might interrupt, a short prayer is enough.
Rabbi Yose draws the rules out plainly: don't go into a ruin; you may pray on the road; on the road, keep it short. Then Elijah asks what he heard.

A heavenly voice, Rabbi Yose says, cooing like a dove, mourning: woe to the children, because of whose sins I destroyed my house and sent them into exile. Elijah tells him this isn't the only time the voice is heard.
Rules about prayer and a story of grief, in one conversation, at one doorway.
One reading: law tells you what to do at a given hour of the night, and story tells you why the night matters at all. Without the law, the story floats. Without the story, the law can go cold.

how: Students learn the Talmud's aggadah in the same study session as its legal discussions, since they appear together on the page; some collections, like the Ein Yaakov, gather the stories on their own.

games.q: you're Rabbi Yose. you've just come out of a ruin where you prayed, and Elijah is waiting at the door. what does Elijah say first?
o: praise you for finding a holy place to pray.
ask why you went in: you could have prayed on the road, briefly.
games.why: Elijah starts with practical advice: don't enter a ruin; you may pray on the road; a short prayer is enough there. only then does he ask what you heard. law and story at one doorway.

practice: See the broken walls, the man praying alone, and the figure waiting at the doorway without interrupting, and hear, if you can, a sound like a dove.

Notice what that doorway held: a rule you can keep, pray where it's safe and keep it short on the road, and a grief no rule can hold. Then ask whether any habit in your own life carries a story like that underneath.
